facts.statement: Hesperogavialis was an extinct genus belonging to the gryposuchine subfamily of gavialids.
facts.quote: Hesperogavialis is an extinct genus of gryposuchine gavialid.

facts.statement: Fossils of Hesperogavialis have been found in Venezuela and Brazil and date from the Middle to Late Miocene.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found from Venezuela and Brazil that date back to the Middle to Late Miocene.

facts.statement: The genus Hesperogavialis possibly comprises three species.
facts.quote: The genus possibly comprises three species.

facts.statement: The type species, H. cruxenti, was found in the Urumaco Formation in Venezuela.
facts.quote: The type species, H. cruxenti, has been found in the Urumaco Formation in Venezuela.

facts.statement: A third species has been recognized from the Solimões Formation in Acre, but it has not yet been formally named.
facts.quote: A third species can be recognized from the same locality in Acre, although a formal name has yet to be given to it.

facts.statement: The posterior portion of the Hesperogavialis skull is unknown, making its classification within the family more difficult than for other gavialoids.
facts.quote: the posterior portion of the skull is still unknown, making any attempts at classification within the family somewhat more difficult than other gavialoids

facts.statement: Hesperogavialis is classified within the family Gavialidae.
Hesperogavialis belongs to the subfamily Gryposuchinae.
The genus Hesperogavialis was described by Bocquetin and Buffetaut in 1981.
The name H. bocquentini was proposed by Sousa-Filho in 1999 but is considered a nomen nudum.
It is debated whether Hesperogavialis is more closely related to the extant Asian Gavialis than to other South American gryposuchines.
facts.quote: Hesperogavialis may actually have had closer relations to the extant Gavialis known from Asia.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the relationship between Hesperogavialis and Asian Gavialis implies multiple dispersal events from the Old World to South America.
facts.quote: This close relationship suggests that there may have been multiple gavialid dispersal events from the Old World to South America.

facts.statement: Some researchers propose that the traits linking Hesperogavialis to Asian gavialoids are independently derived characteristics unique to the genus.
facts.quote: It has also been proposed that this is just an independently derived characteristic unique to Hesperogavialis among the gryposuchines

facts.statement: Hesperogavialis lived between 11.63 and 5.333 million years ago during the Tortonian to Messinian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Tortonian to Messinian (11.63 to 5.333 million years ago)

rejected.quote: A second possible species, named H. bocquentini, has been described from the Solimões Formation in Acre, Brazil.
